newsitem.title: UK: MARK DRIFTS ON CROSSES, UNDECIDED OVER BUBA POLICY.
newsitem.headline: MARK DRIFTS ON CROSSES, UNDECIDED OVER BUBA POLICY.

text.p: The mark drifted aimlessly against its European crosses on Friday, after comments from a Bundesbank official threw more uncertainty over the chance of a change in repo rate policy next week.
With a lack of economic data for traders to chew on, analysts said the market tone was quiet and listless ahead of the Bundesbank's repo announcement next Tuesday.
"There's going to be very little action today," said Ernesto Ramirez, European economist at Bankers Trust in London.
"All we've seen is a little bit of short covering of the EMS currencies versus the mark."

The mark initially pushed higher after Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said on German radio the central bank had already signalled the dollar's correction against the mark was completed at a rate of 1.70 marks. He added that the Bundesbank was watching forex developments "very closely".

The mark's slide to near-eight-year lows against the dollar has fanned speculation that the Bundesbank will allow money-market rates to drift higher by switching to variable-rate tenders from fixed-rate tenders.

But Welteke then said the bank would not change interest rates while there was no sign of inflationary pressure, noting that the impact of exchange rates on the cost of living was extremely small. He added that high German unemployment did not allow them to "turn the interest rate screw".
Analysts said the comments sent a mixed message to traders, most of whom focused on the latter remarks, and bet against a repo rate increase next week.
Ramirez said although he disagreed, the majority of dealers had taken the comments to mean there would not be a rate hike.
"The market is fully on board there won't be a change," he said. "That may lead to a bit of mark softening on the crosses."
In early European trade, however, little movement was seen.
The mark fell against the dollar, after firming momentarily on Welteke's first remark, but barely faltered in Europe.
"Within the EMS grid the remarks didn't have much effect at all," said a dealer at an American bank in London.
"The main impact has been on dollar, sterling and yen as that's where the liquidity is."
Mark/lira slipped slightly to 977.35/65 from 977.80/8.00 late on Thursday, with no reaction seen on Italy's stronger than expected June industrial production figures.
But the mark was little changed versus the French franc, standing at 3.3728/33 compared to 3.3731/34, despite France's current account coming out above expectations.
Sterling firmed up versus the mark, after losing ground on Thursday when the Bank of England raised interest rates by a quarter point but indicated it would be the last raise for some time.
Ramirez said he saw sterling/mark holding around the 3.0 level for the near future, since Britain may still be obliged to increase rates by another 50 basis points before the year end.
However, for EMS currencies, all eyes would remain on the Bundesbank for direction, traders said.
"A lot of people are getting confused about what the Bundesbank's policy is," said the trader at the American bank.
"Personally, I don't think they're going to adjust interest rates to control currency rates -- I think they'll do it from looking at inflation and the economy."
Ramirez said if Germany did surprise the markets with a change in monetary policy, any mark gains were likely to be short-lived.

"There would be a knee-jerk reaction initially, but once people realised the mark's weakness is not because of lack of Bundesbank credibility but is due to concern over the EMU, then I think the dollar will continue to climb against European currencies - in particular the mark - very substantially," he said.
